15.0.0.en: Samuel reminded Saul that God was the One who anointed him to fulfill His will. He said this before asking of him what God had commanded in the following verses.

15.1.0.en: Amalek: a mighty people who dwelt in Sinai and the south of Palestine.

15.1.1.en: God reminds Saul of what Amalek did when he resisted the people of God in the wilderness of Sinai and tried to destroy them, but God intervened and supported Joshua and Moses, so they overcame Amalek (Ex 17), and now the time has come to punish wicked Amalek.

15.2.0.en: For this reason the Lord commanded that Amalek be smitten and avenged upon, and that all he has be killed, men, women, children and beasts, to remove evil and everything connected with it, so that the people of God might know the gravity of evil and its punishment and keep away from it.

15.3.0.en: Footmen: that is, one who walks on his feet and does not ride a horse like the horsemen.

15.3.1.en: Saul obeyed at once and began to gather a great army in the town of Telaim, which is located south of the land of the tribe of Judah, and he numbered the people gathered for war, who were two hundred thousand footmen from all the tribes. The inspired text mentions the number of the men of Judah separately, which was ten thousand men, a small number in comparison with the size of the great tribe, and this shows that the tribe of Judah was still murmuring at the choice of Saul as king from a small tribe, the tribe of Benjamin, so their cooperation with them was limited.

15.3.2.en: It appears here that the number of Saul’s army had become great, two hundred thousand, whereas it is mentioned in (ch. 13:15) that the number of his army was 600 men. The meaning of this is that not a few years had passed between these two events.

15.4.0.en: The Amalekites had no town or city, for they were like roaming Bedouin, and what is meant by the city of Amalek is their land where they had settled and pitched their tents. As for Saul, he hid with his soldiers around them, awaiting the best time to attack them.

15.5.0.en: There was a kinship between the Jews and the Kenites, because Moses married the daughter of Jethro, who was of the Kenites (Ex 3:1), and his son Hobab accompanied them in the wilderness of Sinai (Num 10:29), in addition to the fact that Jael the wife of Heber the Kenite helped the children of Israel by killing Sisera, their enemy (Judg 4:11). For this reason Saul asked the Kenites, who were dwelling beside Amalek, to depart from them lest they be destroyed with them in the war, and they departed.

15.6.0.en: Havilah: a wide land that occupied the region from present-day Kuwait and extended toward the land of the Arabs to the south, that is, the south of Palestine.

15.6.1.en: Shur: it is the wilderness of Shur, and it was west of Havilah and extended opposite Egypt on its east.

15.6.2.en: Saul waged war and attacked all the land of Amalek with his great army, and it was a war extending from the southeast of Palestine to the far west opposite Egypt, because the Amalekites had no fixed cities but were spread out in the desert exactly like Bedouin.

15.7.0.en: Agag: a title of the kings of Amalek, like Pharaoh for the kings of Egypt.

15.7.1.en: Saul was victorious in his war and was able to capture Agag, the greatest of the kings of Amalek, and kill all the people with the edge of the sword, but he disobeyed the Lord’s command to devote everything to destruction, and spared Agag and did not kill him. He also sorted out the spoil he had obtained and devoted to destruction (that is, slaughtered and killed) everything in it that was bad and worthless, but what was good and fair in his eyes he kept and did not destroy, and held it for himself and his men. Perhaps he spared Agag to satisfy his vanity by having a captive king under his hand, or out of pity for this king, and both are disobedience to God. The sparing of the sheep was for the purpose of possessing them and eating of them, and not, as he will claim, that he would offer sacrifices of them to God (v. 15). This shows the extent of his preoccupation with material things and possessions more than with obeying God. And if someone asks why animals that have not sinned are killed, we say that sin is the cause of the ruin of man and of all creation, and then we ask why Christ died although He was innocent! He died to lift sin and its effects from us, from man and from all creation, so that everything may be blessed.

15.7.2.en: However great the power of evil, it is nothing before the power of God, so do not fear the wicked, but hold fast to the truth and trust that God protects you and crushes the demons under your feet.

15.8.0.en: It repented Me: God was no longer pleased and grieved because of Saul’s actions.

15.8.1.en: He was grieved: he was greatly pained because of Saul’s disobedience.

15.8.2.en: He has turned back from following Me: he did not follow what I commanded.

15.8.3.en: The Lord spoke in a vision to His prophet Samuel and told him of His grief because of Saul’s disobedience and that He had rejected him as king of Israel, because Saul despised the word of the Lord and did not devote to destruction the king of Amalek or the good of the spoil but kept them. Of course this was Saul’s second great error after his first error at Gilgal, when he presumed against the priesthood and hastily offered the sacrifice, which is the work of the priests only. As for Samuel, the faithful servant of his people, he grieved greatly when he heard this and continued all night praying earnestly to God to have mercy on his people and forgive Saul.

15.9.0.en: Carmel: about 11.5 km south of Hebron (the present city of Al-Khalil).

15.9.1.en: Samuel did not taste sleep all night, and because of his burning heart he rose very early to meet Saul and asked where he was, and learned that he had gone to Carmel after the battle and set up a pillar or memorial of his victory over Amalek, and then moved on to Gilgal near Jericho. This shows that Saul had begun to boast in his glories and victories in pride, although he had disobeyed God and become rejected by Him.

15.10.0.en: When Samuel arrived at Gilgal, Saul met him joyful and exulting at his coming and at his victory over Amalek, and addressed him, saying, “Blessed are you, O man of God, for I have carried out what God commanded me, and the Lord has given me victory.”

15.11.0.en: Samuel did not return the greeting because of his anger at Saul, but exposed Saul’s disobedience and asked him, if he had carried out the Lord’s command, what then of the bleating of the sheep and the lowing of the cattle that he hears?!!

15.12.0.en: Saul answered him, not realizing the extent of the error committed, that they had taken this spoil from the Amalekites and the people had decided not to destroy all of it but kept the best of it after they had also destroyed much of it.

15.12.1.en: And in a naive attempt by Saul to appease Samuel, he told him that the reason for not killing the cattle was to offer them to the Lord as sacrifices.

15.12.2.en: This shows Saul’s pride, his lack of repentance and his justifying his error by the following:

15.12.3.en: 1- He attributed the error of sparing the sheep to the people and not to himself, although it was he who commanded them to do so. So he is not repentant of the sin.

15.12.4.en: 2- He made an excuse for disobeying God and sparing the sheep, which was offering them as sacrifices to God.

15.12.5.en: 3- He said “the Lord your God” in his speech with Samuel, as if he were saying: if we are pleasing your God, why are you angry? And he did not say “the Lord my God,” which means his separation from God and his not thinking of Him.

15.13.0.en: Decisively Samuel said to Saul, “Enough speaking, and now listen to what the Lord has sent me to say to you this night.”

15.14.0.en: Samuel began the word of the Lord to Saul by reminding him of his beginning, that he was of the smallest of the tribes and the smallest of the clans and nothing at all, but God chose him and made him king over all and the holder of the greatest position and honor among all the people. God also was the One who sent him and charged him with the mission of fighting the Amalekites and gave him victory over them, and God’s request of him was clear, to kill all human beings and beasts and spare none of them.

15.15.0.en: You swooped down on the spoil: you rushed in with a desire to possess the spoil.

15.15.1.en: And now you preferred to keep the spoil, and what you did was a great evil which angered the Lord against you and made Him reject you.

15.16.0.en: The best of the things devoted to destruction: the firstlings of the cattle and sheep which God had devoted to destruction.

15.16.1.en: Saul did not offer anything new in his speech, but said, in a new self-deception and an attempt to lessen the accusation, that he had done nothing but God’s command to fight Amalek and be victorious over them, and that their king “Agag” was captured and all his people killed, and he had not spared of the cattle except their firstlings and best so as to offer them as sacrifices to the Lord at Gilgal. Of course this was an error, because God does not accept sacrifices from animals which He had previously asked to be devoted to destruction. This shows Saul’s persistence in pride and in justifying himself and his complete distance from repentance and seeking God’s mercies. Saul said to Samuel “the Lord your God,” and did not say “the Lord our God,” and this shows his separation from God and his lack of sonship to Him.

15.17.0.en: To convince Saul of the gravity of his error, Samuel asked him a question of rebuke, saying to him, which is better with God: to listen to His word and carry out His commands exactly as He said them, or to offer sacrifices while disobeying Him?! And Samuel answered his own question, that listening and submitting to God’s commands is far better than offering rams and sacrifices.

15.18.0.en: Divination: an attempt to know the unseen by means of Satan.

15.18.1.en: Teraphim: small statues or miniature models of pagan gods which the pagans keep in their houses to seek blessing from them.

15.18.2.en: Samuel continued his speech and rebuke to Saul, making clear to him that what he had done was rebellion and defiance of the Lord’s command, and that by his foolishness and lack of submission he was as if he had fallen into the sin of divination or idolatry, and because he rejected obeying God, the Lord also rejected him from leading this people.

15.18.3.en: Many people do exactly as Saul did: they hate others and wrong them and then give much money and many gifts to the Church ... Do not be deceived, beloved, but first learn to love others and forgive them, and after this offer what you wish to offer, and know well that God cannot be deceived or bribed.

15.19.0.en: After Saul’s failed attempts at defense, and his attempt to pin the accusation on the people, and in the face of Samuel’s clear and frank words about Saul’s violations of all God’s word and his announcement of God’s judgment on him and his rejection as king of Israel, Saul began to offer an apology and declared his error and his breaking of God’s commandments. He offered an excuse worse than the offense, namely that the king and victorious commander feared the people and allowed them, and by this apology he was only adding a new offense to his offenses. He begged Samuel to forgive him and to go with him before God’s altar set up at Gilgal so that he might worship the Lord repentant and sorrowful, although his real intention was not repentance and submission to God, but that Samuel should accompany him as he entered the house of the Lord so that the people would be sure that he was still king and God was pleased with him, which was the opposite of the truth.

15.19.1.en: If you err, do not try to justify yourself, but in humility express sorrow for what came from you, and you will receive God’s forgiveness and the respect of others, for they will feel that you are bearing responsibility, so they will trust you and deal with you at ease.

15.20.0.en: Samuel refused Saul’s plea and was decisive in his words, and made clear to Saul that the matter was not in his hand but in the hand of God, who had rejected him, and therefore he too could not go against God and His commands.

15.21.1.en: Samuel wanted to depart from Saul and from the place, and when he turned to go on his way, Saul seized the hem of his outer garment tightly and the skirt of the garment was torn. Samuel took the tearing of his robe as a prophetic sign and told Saul that just as his garment had been torn in two, so God would remove Saul from his people Israel and give the kingdom to another person, who is better than he before God. The word “neighbor” means of course the person of David the prophet, whom Saul loved at first and gave in marriage to his daughter Michal, as we shall see in the events of the book (ch. 16:21, ch. 18:20).

15.22.0.en: The Strength of Israel: the God of Israel, who counsels and guides him.

15.22.1.en: Will not repent: He does not draw back from His decision to reject Saul, because He is God who knows all things. God’s repenting in (v. 11) is an expression meaning His displeasure with Saul, because God chose him when he was humble, but he became proud and disobeyed God, so God rejected him; and when God rejected him, this was not a hasty decision, but God announced His decision with the utmost wisdom, understanding and justice. God uses words that we know as human beings, namely repentance, but what is meant by God’s repenting, as we mentioned in (v. 11), is His displeasure.

15.22.2.en: Samuel continues his speech to Saul, saying that God is the One who announced your rejection and your removal from the throne of the kingdom, and God is far above lying or repenting, for He is not like a man who takes a decision in an hour of anger and then repents afterward, but is an almighty God of all knowledge, and His declared will has no turning back.

15.23.0.en: Saul confessed his error, but he cared more about his appearance before the elders and the people than about God’s punishment of him and rejection of him, so he pressed Samuel to return with him and worship before God for the sake of his honor and appearance and so that no one would know of the divine punishment and God’s rejection of him. His purpose was not repentance but keeping up his appearance as king. And he did not say “the people of God” but “my people,” which shows his arrogance, his selfishness and his lack of submission to God, for he ascribes the people to himself and not to God.

15.24.0.en: In the face of Saul’s continued pressing, and perhaps because of the kindness of Samuel’s heart, we find that Samuel did indeed turn back and return with Saul to the house of the Lord, where Saul worshiped.

15.25.0.en: After Saul’s worship, Samuel did not forget God’s command to devote to destruction, and for this reason he gave the order to bring Agag king of Amalek. As for Agag, when he learned that Samuel had summoned him, it did not occur to him what he would do to him, but he rejoiced and thought that he would be released from captivity, and for this reason he said to himself that at last the specter of death would depart from him.

15.26.0.en: Childless: the woman who has lost her son.

15.26.1.en: Before the Lord: before the house of the Lord, to carry out God’s command before His house.

15.26.2.en: When they brought Agag before Samuel, Samuel said to him, in an introduction before issuing his sentence, that just as your sword was the cause of killing many men and young men and made their mothers childless, weeping for their children, so today your mother will be childless and weep for you all the days of her life; and after that Samuel commanded that Agag’s head be cut off, and all this was done at Gilgal before Samuel left.

15.26.3.en: Agag is a symbol of the great sin which a person must cut off from his life, however much it is bound up with things dear to him, because obeying God is better than anything.

15.27.0.en: Samuel returned to Ramah, which was his town and place of residence, while Saul went up to his house and family in his place of residence at Gibeah of Saul.

15.28.0.en: The meeting between Saul and Samuel at Gilgal was the last of the meetings that brought them together, and Samuel did not see Saul again all his life, since he knew the Lord’s decision concerning him, but he wept much in his prayer for Saul and over how the first king of Israel had become rejected. The expression that the Lord repented that He had made Saul king is meant to confirm God’s rejection and the appointment, in the divine purpose, of another man to reign over Israel. The meaning of God’s rejection of Saul is His refusal that he be king over His people, but Samuel continued to weep over him, asking for his repentance, that perhaps he might repent as a human being and not lose his eternity, but unfortunately he continued in his evils until the end of his life.

15.28.1.en: Be obedient to God’s commands in declaring the truth and being firm with those who err, for pity on evil increases it and makes others stumble, so that it becomes a sin ... And do not do your own will but the will of God.

15.28.2.en: The anointing of David as king
